<figure class="diagram-figure"><p class="diagram-title">One cycle of PCR</p><img class="diagram-image diagram-light" src="/diagrams/germomics-52d7f101-light.svg" alt="Denature leads to Anneal, which leads to Extend, which leads to Repeat. Denature is heat separating the two DNA strands. Anneal is primers binding, at a temperature that depends on the primers. Extend is Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, copying each strand and staying active through the heat. Repeat is those copies becoming templates." role="img" width="168" height="320" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><img class="diagram-image diagram-dark" src="/diagrams/germomics-52d7f101-dark.svg" alt="Denature leads to Anneal, which leads to Extend, which leads to Repeat. Denature is heat separating the two DNA strands. Anneal is primers binding, at a temperature that depends on the primers. Extend is Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, copying each strand and staying active through the heat. Repeat is those copies becoming templates." role="img" width="168" height="320" loading="lazy" decoding="async"><figcaption><p>A schematic of that order, not a temperature protocol and not a count of product. A real reaction does not double the target at every cycle.</p><p>Sources: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.2448875">Saiki, Gelfand, Stoffel and colleagues, Science (1988)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.127.3.1550-1557.1976">Chien, Edgar and Trela, Journal of Bacteriology (1976)</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0076-6879(87)55023-6">Mullis and Faloona, Methods in Enzymology (1987)</a>.</p></figcaption></figure>
